P1.evidence: The weakest opening in the batch. No frame was set at all — not two-part, not any part — and no frame agreement was sought. The setter was discussed socially rather than read back, and the prospect summarised his own call with Kyla. The first five minutes ran as unstructured conversation with the prospect talking while he showered and took a work call, and the rep said so out loud: "I'm not telling you... I don't know what the I'm doing, to be honest with you. I'm just letting you talk, brother." The scripted open question never came; what eventually redirected the call was "Well, like, give me an overview. Where are you at right now?", which is a baseline prompt, not the open. Scored a miss on process; the call recovered strongly afterwards, which does not change what happened here.

P2.evidence: One clean hit. The single open prompt at 00:05:14 did a lot of work — it produced height, weight, age, work history and the training week in one answer ("I'm 5'11". I weighed myself last night. I'm 188... I'm working out at least three times a week... And then I run frequently") — but that is the prospect volunteering, not the rep working through the checks. Nothing was asked about health conditions, injuries, chronic pain or movement limitations at any point on a call with a 47-year-old. Diet was never asked; he raised it himself at 00:28:44 ("a thing I struggle with too is the nutrition end of things") and the rep's entire response was "It's easy stuff, brother. We'll just fix it." No sleep, no energy, no results from current training.

P3.evidence: The best goals work in the batch by a clear margin, and it is the reason this call is still alive. The scaling question ran (6.5 out of 10), then the bridge, in three words: "What would change if you had that?" That opened the wife, the confidence, and the beach at Cape May. The rep then drove all the way to identity, which nobody else in this batch did: "it's clear that you're successful... You figured out how to overcome substances and alcohol. Why do you feel like you haven't been able to do that with this area?" followed by the perfect-version-of-yourself question, which produced the prospect's own verdict — "You're slacking. You're using work as an excuse to not go downstairs and sweat it out." Two reflect-backs landed, the second of them the sharpest line on any call in the batch: "you do everything for everybody else. And maybe there's a part of you that feels like doing something for yourself is selfish" — "Yeah, possibly." Marked down only on 'something physical you can't do', never asked, and 'who else does that impact', which arrived because the prospect volunteered his wife and daughter rather than because the rep asked.

P4.evidence: Properly run. The rep asked why directly and more than once — "Why, though?" about the fifteen-year unused gym membership, and "Why do you feel like you haven't been able to do that with this area? And the reason why I ask is because for us to be able to help you overcome that, kind of got to need to know what the block is." The prospect named the gap himself and named it precisely: "I need more structure, you know? That's what I'm lacking. I mean, it's, I'm all over the place, dude." The rep's framing that people live in patterns and "you have to punch the pattern in the face if you want to change it" is a serviceable variant of the P4f move. Past attempts were mapped loosely rather than sequenced, which is the only real gap.

P5.evidence: The only call in the batch where any consequence framing ran at all. The rep picked up the prospect's own fear of sudden decline and made it two-directional: "there's an up that I can go to, but there's also a down that I can go to if I don't, like, get in control" and "Well, that's good, because you get to choose which one you have." He later named the trap precisely: "you're not where you want to be, but you're not dying. And I think that part of you is like, because it's not that bad, it kind of stops you from having that push towards fixing it." The 'willing to settle' check ran as a consented challenge — "Do you feel resistance if I say to you, when it comes to your health and fitness, you're average, bang average?" — and got the phase's real payload: "No, I'm not offended at all. I agree with you. I concur... I'm embarrassed." What is still missing is the two-year projection, the 'why not', and a hard line in the sand; "Do you feel like you're ready to commit to overcoming them?" is the nearest thing and it drew a hedge.

P6.evidence: The all-in question ran, and unusually for this batch the rep refused to accept a soft answer: "Is this something you're definitely all in on, definitely going to do?" — "Yeah, I think so, man." — "You think so?" — "I think so." — "You think?" That is the check working as designed. The capacity gate also ran before presenting ("can you make 45 minutes a day, four days a week?"), as did a commitment probe ("Do you feel like you're ready to commit to overcoming them?") which drew "Yeah. I mean, we'll see. I mean, I think so." The problem is what happened next: hesitation surfaced and the rep presented anyway rather than returning to phase 5, which is exactly what P6c prohibits. He then had to come back and do the phase-5 work retrospectively, after the price.

P11.evidence: No step completed for the programme. The $6,000 was not collected and no payment link for it was sent; what was sent and paid was a $100 refundable deposit to hold the next day's call. The Trevor onboarding call was named as Monday but never booked. No agreement email, nothing signed, no welcome email, Skool link or questionnaire. The rep did explain the onboarding sequence clearly and did ask for the money ("we'd just process it now. Just credit card, debit card, visa"), so the attempt was made; it simply did not land.

objection_plays.detail: "Let me speak to my wife and tell her that my trainer is going to be more than hers." The most complete play run anywhere in this batch. What ran: the test of whether her answer actually matters ("What if she doesn't [agree]?" — "No, no, she will. She doesn't have a choice"); the necessity challenge, twice ("Can I challenge you? Do you really need to speak to her?"); the is-this-input-or-permission frame in the prospect's own words ("even though I'm the breadwinner, you know, I've succumbed to still having to speak to, you know, making decisions with finances"); the hesitation probe ("If she says no, you'll do it anyway. Like what's really coming up for you?"); and the scripted deposit fallback, executed live — "I want to challenge you to put a hundred buck deposit down. And if worst case scenario, she says no, or whatever, we can refund it." Not run: 'money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal' and 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger'. The second of those was sitting right there, given a wife who spends $700 a month on her own trainer.

"Let's see. Let's see what happens here." The rep did the hardest part — he named the evasion rather than accepting it: "So there is something coming up. Be real with me, James. Just be real" — and repeated the probe later. What did not run is the rest of the sequence: no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and no 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now', which is a striking omission given that the rep had spent ten minutes constructing exactly that man in phase 3.

Handled cleverly and pre-emptively rather than by the book. Before quoting anything the rep asked "What if it doesn't fit in the budget? What happens then?", which drew the prospect's own ceiling — "if it's a couple grand, it's not a problem. If we're talking $10,000, $12,000..." — so the $6,000 landed inside a range the prospect had already set. It worked: "That's not terrible. My wife pays 700 a month for her guy." But no isolate ran, no financial picture was taken in any dimension, and when the price was later reframed by the prospect as "a bit much" the rep did not return to it.

Script gap and a commercial one. The prospect's wife pays $700 a month to a private trainer, trains seriously, and is the benchmark he measures himself against — he raised her four separate times. There is no play, and no attempt, for the household or partner opportunity, and no attempt to use her as an ally in the spouse objection either. The obvious question — is there any reason your wife, who spends $8,400 a year on her own coach, would object to you spending $6,000 on yours — was never asked.

notes: Two different calls stitched together. The first five minutes are the loosest opening in the batch, with no frame, no agreement and the rep openly narrating that he was just letting the prospect talk. Everything from 00:07 onward is the best work in the batch: a real bridge, genuine identity work, a consequence frame that actually ran, an all-in question that refused a soft yes, and a full OB play ending in the scripted deposit. The one process error that cost the close is P6c — hesitation surfaced before the presentation and he presented anyway, then had to do the phase-5 work backwards after the price. Set the frame, and go back to five when the yes is soft.
